items.title: Today’s price action highlights the resilience of the US equity market: It has contained losses to under 1% so far, even as oil has surged 6% and 10-year Treasury yields have jumped 11 bps. Impressive corporate earnings have provided vital insulation for the stock market, alongside the remarkably limited spillover—so far—from interest rate risk to credit risk. How this evolves will largely depend on whether higher yields weaken the economy, reduce financing availability, and/or trigger pockets of deleveraging. #economy #stocks #investing #investors #markets #bonds

items.title: The UK gilt market’s high beta is on display again today as 10-year yields surge to nearly 5.40% amid this global sell-off—and this in the run-up to the government delivering its first, highly anticipated budget on October 28. For the reasons detailed in my April Financial Times column on "who lost the UK bond market" (link below), this structural vulnerability has been building for years and now has self-feeding dynamics: sluggish productivity colliding with expanding deficits and the refinancing of debt last incurred at lower borrowing costs, making both economic growth and fiscal sustainability even harder to achieve.

items.content:
Among the things to watch this morning in markets and the global economy:
US PPI Inflation: The consensus forecasts are for a 0.4% monthly jump in headline PPI (lifting the annual inflation rate to 5.3%) and a 0.3% rise in core (4.6%). These readings will come ahead of tomorrow’s CPI inflation report.
ECB Rate Decision: Beyond a widely anticipated 25 bps rate hike, all eyes will be on the accompanying remarks, particularly how European central bankers characterize the inflation dynamics and the appetite for further tightening.
Meanwhile, markets are brushing aside the administration’s $5,000 “voter dividend” proposal, viewing actual implementation as highly improbable against a 6% budget deficit, solid growth, and pressure from elevated sovereign bond yields.
 #economy   #markets   #ecb   #inflation   #ppi 
— Mohamed A. El-Erian (@elerianm) Sep 10, 2026

items.content:
When it comes to the Federal Reserve, markets are understandably focused on whether the world's most powerful central bank hikes next week and, if it does, whether it is a "one and done" or the start of a cycle.
Yet, for the reasons I have detailed in a prior column, the more consequential question for the economy and markets is the extent to which the new chair, Kevin Warsh, succeeds in reforming how the Fed operates and, in this context, minimizing the risk of repeating the policy slippages of recent years.
In this regard, media outlets report more support internally for reducing the number of FOMC rate-setting meetings from eight to six and scheduling two dedicated strategy meetings instead.
 #economy   #federalreserve   #markets 
— Mohamed A. El-Erian (@elerianm) Sep 9, 2026
